transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-04-25
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Jenna Ortiz (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Vela CTO), Priya Singh (Vela ML Eng), Carlos Gomez (Vela Infra)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping to define latency and throughput SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), size the workload, agree benchmark plan and timeline. Customer wants clear success criteria for go/no-go and a measurement plan covering warm vs cold cache and tail percentiles.

Topics:
- Define TTFT (time-to-first-token) vs TPOT (time-per-token) and targets (p95/p99)
- Workload sizing: concurrent users, token lengths, burst patterns
- Benchmark plan: synthetic traces + replay of real traces, warm/cold cache, quantization profiles
- Timeline and next steps for initial POC run

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for doing this, um this should be a quick scoping, objective is to lock down the latency SLOs and measurement plan for the POC, does that sound right to you Marka— Mark?
[00:10] Mark: yeah that's right, sorry bit of audio lag, yes we're mainly concerned about tail latency for our assistant product, users notice any lag, it's very noticeable.
[00:20] Jenna: cool, quick intro, i'm jenna on the se team, i'll own the benchmark runs with samir, and we'll propose the scripts and configs.
[00:28] Priya: quick context, our prod workload is ~600 qps at peak across 3 regions today, average prompt length around 60 tokens but we have about 10% of requests that are 250+ tokens, and we do a few-shot prompt for some customers so those are heavier. We're looking at both chat style real-time replies and batch scoring for internal workflows.
[00:45] Carlos: infra constraints — we want to keep traffic inside our VPC during the pilot, and we have 1Gbps interconnect to the region, also need to understand egress and TLS handoff.
[00:56] Samir: perfect, that's helpful. let's start with definitions so we're all aligned: TTFT we define as time from request ingress at the inference gateway to the first byte of the model response (first token). TPOT is the time-per-token once streaming begins — basically token service time. folks comfortable with those defs?
[01:12] Mark: yes that's fine. i sometimes see vendors call it "time to first byte" or mix terms, so thanks for being explicit.
[01:20] Jenna: note — transcription might call TTFT as T T F T in some notes, ignore that.
[01:24] Priya: what about setup — do you measure from our app's egress or from your gateway?
[01:28] Samir: good question — for apples-to-apples we propose measuring both: from your app (end-to-end) and from our gateway (service-only). the POC should include both so we can isolate network vs model/runtime.
[01:36] Jenna: and we'll provide scripts that can run inside your VPC to replay traces so the e2e numbers are reproducible.
[01:42] Mark: great. ok target SLOs — our internal bar for launch would be p95 TTFT under 200ms and p99 under 400ms for chat interactions. for TPOT we want p95 under 60ms and p99 under 150ms when the KV cache is warm. are those realistic?
[01:58] Jenna: reasonable as a starting point depending on model size and instance type. for example on an 8xA100 with FP16 and optimized kernels we often hit p95 TTFT ~120-180ms for short prompts and TPOT p95 ~30-50ms. for quantized int8 sometimes TPOT improves but cold cache and compilation spikes can add to TTFT.
[02:17] Priya: ok can you explain the warm vs cold cache effect in practice?
[02:20] Jenna: yeah, so warm cache means the KV cache for the model is populated and JIT/kernels compiled. cold means first requests may trigger compilation and KV miss that add tens to hundreds of ms. we usually measure both as separate test cases: cold-start window and steady-state window.
[02:34] Samir: important note — TTFT and TPOT behave differently with batching. large batching can improve throughput (tokens/sec) but increase TTFT. so part of the SLO tradeoff is latency vs unit cost.
[02:45] Mark: our product is latency-sensitive, so we'd prefer single-request low-latency mode over high batch throughput. but we need cost visibility, so tradeoffs are needed.
[02:53] Jenna: understood — for the POC we'll run two profiles: "low-latency" (batch size 1, minimal queueing) and "throughput" (aggressive batching). we'll measure TTFT and TPOT p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[03:06] Priya: what about sequence length and TPOT? longer responses obviously increase total time, but per-token time also can vary?
[03:11] Jenna: per-token time is usually stable once streaming starts but transformer KV lookups and attention window effects can slightly increase TPOT for very long histories. we'll include length-bucketed percentiles (e.g., <=50, 51-150, >150 tokens).
[03:25] Carlos: regarding load — we have diurnal peaks and short bursts, how should you simulate that?
[03:29] Samir: we'll replay real traces you provide and also run synthetic burst tests: constant QPS, 10s/30s bursts, and step tests (ramping QPS) to validate autoscale behavior and tail.
[03:38] Samir: measurement plan outline, high level:
- replay representative production traces (you provide) inside your VPC for e2e;
- run service-only tests from our gateway to isolate runtime;
- run cold-start window tests (empty cache, cold kernels) and steady-state warm cache tests;
- run both low-latency (batch=1) and throughput (opt batching) profiles;
- collect p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, plus tokens/sec and error rates;
- produce histograms and percentile timelines (5-min windows) so we can spot spikes.
[04:05] Priya: that sounds good. how long will each phase take?
[04:08] Jenna: initial script runs can be done in a day but to get stable p99 numbers we prefer repeated runs across different time windows — recommend 2-3 hours per profile for robust tails, but initial runs we can do in 1-2 hours to surface major issues. total initial benchmarking ~ 1 week with run scheduling.
[04:21] Mark: timeline wise we want a pilot within two weeks; POC completion in 4 weeks and then decide on dedicated capacity. is that feasible?
[04:29] Samir: yes that's in line with similar customers. we'll aim to run the first bench in the coming week and review results next Wednesday.
[04:35] Jenna: config details we'll test: model variants (e.g., 13B fp16, 13B int8), quantization profiles, KV cache warm/cold, batch sizes (1, 8, 32), sequence lengths, and request concurrency (25, 50, 100 concurrent).
[04:47] Priya: can you also measure tail contributions from networking and TLS handshake?
[04:50] Samir: yes we'll capture both application-level timings and tcp/tls timings where possible. if you run the e2e inside VPC we can correlate network spans. we'll also run service-only from our gateway to subtract network effects.
[04:59] Carlos: from infra side, we need to understand SLOs under our autoscaler rules. if we hit p99 spikes we need to be able to scale quickly. how does Redwood handle autoscale and burst?
[05:08] Jenna: Redwood Dedicated supports configurable autoscale policies and burst capacity; for the POC we'll test cold-scaling (spin-up latency) and warm-burst capacity to ensure we don't violate p99 SLOs. note spin-up of additional instances can take tens of seconds, so workload shaping/backpressure matters.
[05:21] Mark: what about metrics we should expect to receive and dashboards?
[05:24] Samir: we'll provide per-route dashboards: TTFT and TPOT histograms, token rate, GPU util, queue lengths, batch sizes, and compilation events. we'll also share the raw logs and a benchmark spreadsheet. link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/vela-initial (placeholder)
[05:36] Priya: any differences between hosted and dedicated numbers we should expect?
[05:39] Jenna: hosted is multi-tenant and we provide performance profiles; Dedicated with pinned GPUs tends to be more predictable for p99s. Private on-prem can add networking variability. POC should include dedicated runs for final decision.
[05:50] Samir: success criteria proposal (customer validation):
- Functional: feature correctness and no increased error rates vs baseline
- Latency: TTFT p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 400ms (chat low-latency profile); TPOT p95 <= 60ms, p99 <= 150ms with warm cache
- Throughput: sustain 50 concurrent interactive sessions with the above SLOs at your average request mix
- Stability: no more than 0.1% error rate and no rolling restarts during test windows
[06:18] Mark: we can accept that as a starting point; might tighten p99 later but good for POC.
[06:23] Priya: what about measuring tokenization differences? we use a custom tokenizer for a subset of customers which changes token counts significantly.
[06:29] Jenna: include tokenization in replay — please share tokenizer or tokenized traces. we'll measure tokens-per-request so TPOT is normalized.
[06:36] Carlos: security note — we need SOC2 docs, SAML/SSO support, and log retention details.
[06:41] Samir: will share security pack and SSO integration guide. we'll also include audit log retention options in the follow-up email.
[06:48] Mark: are there known gotchas — like kernel compile spikes or specific model layers that cause tails?
[06:52] Jenna: yes JIT/kernels and first-time compilation are the most common. also KV cache eviction patterns during long conversations can bump TPOT. another gotcha is batching at the gateway: bursts can create micro-queues that raise TTFT. we'll instrument to find those.
[07:06] Priya: for the measurement plan deliverable can you provide a template SLO doc we can review?
[07:10] Samir: yes we'll share a draft SLO doc with definitions (TTFT/TPOT), measurement windows, and pass/fail rules.
[07:16] Mark: ok last question on reporting — how do you compute p99 across windows, SLO aggregation method?
[07:22] Jenna: we recommend computing p99 on sliding 5-minute windows and then reporting the maximum p99 across the test period for conservative assessment. alternatively report both median p99 and the 95th of p99s, but for decisions we prefer the max p99 observed. we'll include both in the report.
[07:39] Samir: timeline recap: Priya share traces and tokenization by 2027-04-28; Carlos provide network topo by 2027-04-28; Samir to send scripts and security pack by 2027-05-02; Jenna run initial benchmarks by 2027-05-03; review meeting scheduled 2027-05-05.
[07:55] Mark: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[07:58] Priya: one minor nit — please include cold-start 95/99 as a separate metric, otherwise it skews the steady-state numbers.
[08:04] Jenna: will do.
[08:06] Samir: ok wrapping up, we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and bootstrapping instructions, and confirm follow-up time. action items and dates in the meeting notes.
[08:14] Mark: thanks, bye.
